title: Answering negative possession questions
summary: To confirm that someone does have the thing, answer On. To say they do not have it, answer Ei ole.
prerequisiteSkills: Fixed eikö ole in possession questions
objectives: Answer a negative question clearly according to whether the owner has the thing.
Recognise the pattern, then produce it with the supporting words shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: To confirm that someone does have the thing, answer On. To say they do not have it, answer Ei ole.

English yes/no replies to negative questions can be confusing. These tasks state the intended response meaning explicitly. On. / Kyllä, on. confirm possession; Ei ole. / Ei, ei ole. deny it. These verb replies stay fixed for all owners.
keyPoints: Use one singular thing and the owner form shown by the prompt.

sections.title: Regular noun forms in these examples
paragraphs: These forms name the thing after ei ole. The prompts show the noun form whenever forming it is outside this lesson’s target.
keyPoints: kissa (“cat”) → kissaa (“a cat”): regular singular partitive
koira (“dog”) → koiraa (“a dog”): regular singular partitive
tyyny (“pillow”) → tyynyä (“a pillow”): regular singular partitive
peli (“game”) → peliä (“a game”): regular singular partitive

examples.english: Don’t I have a ball? — I do have it.
steps: minulla means “I as the owner”. The question names palloa (“a ball”).
The reply confirms possession, so echo fixed On (“have/has” here).
The short verb reply leaves the understood owner and thing unspoken; do not conjugate it for that owner.
Answer whether the person has the thing: On confirms having it; Ei ole denies it, even after a negative question.

examples.finnish: Eikö sinulla ole kirjaa? — Ei ole.
examples.english: Don’t you have a book? — You do not have it.
steps: sinulla means “you as the owner” for one person. The question names kirjaa (“a book”).
The reply denies possession, so use fixed Ei ole (“do/does not have” here).
The short verb reply leaves the understood owner and thing unspoken; do not conjugate it for that owner.
Answer whether the person has the thing: On confirms having it; Ei ole denies it, even after a negative question.

examples.finnish: Eikö hänellä ole koiraa? — Kyllä, on.
examples.english: Doesn’t she have a dog? — She does have it.
steps: hänellä means “he as the owner” or “she as the owner”; this example uses “she”. The question names koiraa (“a dog”).
The reply confirms possession, so echo fixed On (“have/has” here).
Kyllä (“yes”) is an optional answer particle; On. alone also confirms possession.
Answer whether the person has the thing: On confirms having it; Ei ole denies it, even after a negative question.

examples.finnish: Eikö meillä ole autoa? — Ei, ei ole.
examples.english: Don’t we have a car? — We do not have it.
steps: meillä means “we as the owner”. The question names autoa (“a car”).
The reply denies possession, so use fixed Ei ole (“do/does not have” here).
The first Ei (“no”) is an optional answer particle; Ei ole. alone also denies possession.
Answer whether the person has the thing: On confirms having it; Ei ole denies it, even after a negative question.

examples.english: Don’t you have a game? — You do have it.
steps: teillä means “you as the owner” for a group. The question names peliä (“a game”).
The reply confirms possession, so echo fixed On (“have/has” here).
The short verb reply leaves the understood owner and thing unspoken; do not conjugate it for that owner.
Answer whether the person has the thing: On confirms having it; Ei ole denies it, even after a negative question.

examples.finnish: Eikö heillä ole kynää? — Ei ole.
examples.english: Don’t they have a pen? — They do not have it.
steps: heillä means “they as the owner”. The question names kynää (“a pen”).
The reply denies possession, so use fixed Ei ole (“do/does not have” here).
The short verb reply leaves the understood owner and thing unspoken; do not conjugate it for that owner.
Answer whether the person has the thing: On confirms having it; Ei ole denies it, even after a negative question.

examples.finnish: Eikö minulla ole kissaa? — Kyllä, on.
examples.english: Don’t I have a cat? — I do have it.
steps: minulla means “I as the owner”. The question names kissaa (“a cat”).
The reply confirms possession, so echo fixed On (“have/has” here).
Kyllä (“yes”) is an optional answer particle; On. alone also confirms possession.
Answer whether the person has the thing: On confirms having it; Ei ole denies it, even after a negative question.

examples.finnish: Eikö meillä ole tyynyä? — Ei, ei ole.
examples.english: Don’t we have a pillow? — We do not have it.
steps: meillä means “we as the owner”. The question names tyynyä (“a pillow”).
The reply denies possession, so use fixed Ei ole (“do/does not have” here).
The first Ei (“no”) is an optional answer particle; Ei ole. alone also denies possession.
Answer whether the person has the thing: On confirms having it; Ei ole denies it, even after a negative question.

commonMistakes: A negative question does not reverse the fact: On still confirms having the thing, and Ei ole still denies it.
Keep the reply fixed for every owner; Olemme and Emme ole describe “we are” and “we are not”, rather than possession.
Use the requested verb reply; optional Kyllä or an additional Ei does not replace on or ei ole.
